items.title: ‘No means no, however we dress and wherever we go’: 50 years of campaigning against rape
items.summary:
Grassroots group Women Against Rape says ‘things are really changing’ in how victims are treated by criminal justice system

When Mr Justice Bennathan sentenced Russell Brand to 10 and a half years in prison, there was a notable shift in the characterisation of victims of sexual assault. “Whatever women wear, wherever they go, whatever they drink, they retain the right to say no, and to demand justice from the criminal courts when sexual predators like you, Russell Brand, act without their consent,” the judge said.

In 1977 it was a completely different story. Justices Roskill, Wien and Slynn allowed the convicted rapist Queen’s Guardsman Tom Holdsworth to walk free on appeal after his rape conviction because of his “promising army career”. The same year, Judge Zigmond gave the rapist of a three-year-old girl just a suspended sentence, telling her mother: “You will forget it and so will your little girl.” Judge Peter Mason gave a six-month sentence to Maurice Markham, a rapist from the Royal Navy, because “it would be a shame if the country loses your services”.

Continue reading...
items.t: ‘No means no, however we dress and wherever we go’: 50 years of campaigning against rape

items.title: Consent under scrutiny: where does youth end and adulthood begin?
items.summary:
After the Brand and Walliams revelations, calls for a ‘staggered’ age of consent are redefining what makes someone ‘adult’

The fact that the age of sexual consent in Britain is set at 16 is thanks to a chimney sweep’s daughter from Marylebone, London, called Eliza Armstrong – not that she had any say in the matter.

In June 1885, Armstrong had just turned 13 when she was sold for sex by her alcoholic mother for the sum of £5. She believed she was going to work as a gentleman’s maid; instead, the child was taken to a brothel, where she was examined to prove she was a virgin and drugged with chloroform to await the gentleman who had “purchased” her virginity.

items.title: AI Use Guidelines: It’s Complicated. It’s Also Not A Choice
items.summary:
The other day, I gave a presentation to a group of lawyers and legal professionals about AI use and its benefits and risks. As is my practice, I stressed the need for law firms of any and all sizes to have strong AI-use guidelines. I stressed that these guidelines should cover things like which tools are approved for use, the need to protect confidentiality, and the need to verify all citations and other information from any AI output. 

And of course, I also talked about the risks of not having an AI use policy. The risk of unauthorized or shadow use of unapproved tools, the risk of confidentiality breaches, and the risk of citations to hallucinated cases and propositions. My standard shtick.

But for some reason, it occurred to me right before this presentation that I should also mention an added reason for robust AI use guidelines. And that is that good guidelines could protect a law firm if someone goes rogue and fails to verify citations before filing them in a court document. I usually don’t talk much about this since it seems rather obvious. But as it turns out, I was prescient to do so. 

On November 13, 2026, the Delaware Court of Chancery issued an order sanctioning a lawyer who signed a brief with hallucinated citations. But it exonerated his law firm because it had proper AI use guidelines in place. 

The Wrong Way 

Here’s what happened. A lawyer submitted fabricated quotations and mischaracterized legal authorities in a brief. After he was outed by the other side, he owned up to it. Sort of. He filed a “corrected” brief. That brief removed quotation marks…
items.t: AI Use Guidelines: It’s Complicated. It’s Also Not A Choice

items.title: Some Law Firm Names Are Simply Too Long
items.summary:
Lawyers understandably have a certain amount of pride when it comes to seeing their names on the doors of law firms. Indeed, many lawyers work their entire careers with the hope that they will one day become a named partner of a law firm and have their name adorn letterhead, business cards, and other materials associated with a law practice. Moreover, adding a lawyer’s name a law firm can be an effective way to recognize that attorney’s contributions to a practice without necessarily altering the financial arrangements among the partners. However, some law firm names are simply too long. Law firms should generally have no more than four names for a variety of practical reasons.

Earlier in my career, I worked at a law firm that had four names. Although the name of the firm was somewhat lengthy, it was not particularly difficult to recite the name of the firm when answering the phone or introducing myself to other lawyers. At some point during my tenure at this law firm, the firm added a fifth name.

For whatever reason, adding that fifth name made it exponentially more difficult to say the name of the law firm. One would think that adding another name would only make it marginally more cumbersome to recite the name of the firm. However, there seems to be a point at which a law firm’s name becomes too much of a mouthful, and in my experience, the distinction between four and five names can be surprisingly significant.

This can be especially annoying for lawyers who need to identify themselves and their law firms numerous times throughout the day. When appearing in court,…
items.t: Some Law Firm Names Are Simply Too Long

items.title: DOJ Demand To Hide Misconduct Inside Special Master Fails To Impress Judge
items.summary:
It was another exciting morning for Stan Woodward, the omnipresent associate attorney general, who got reamed out by Judge April Perry in Chicago for being very bad at law … again.

Woodward’s entire job consists of parachuting in to courtrooms where the government is in trouble and making matters so much worse . In Chicago, US Attorney Andrew Boutros’s office was already flailing after being forced to dismiss charges against the “Broadview 6” for obstruction of a government official in the conduct of his duties, i.e., getting hit by an ICE agent’s car in the middle of a protest. The government spent months indignantly denouncing the allegations of prosecutorial misconduct as “fevered paranoia and delusional speculation.” But the unsealed grand jury transcripts showed three separate presentations to the same panel in October of 2025, each of which was plagued by obvious impropriety.

In open court, USA Boutros assured Judge Perry that he only discovered the problem five months later. And his office assured the court that they’d had no discussions with Main Justice about the case. 

Turns out … not so much. 

Boutros was emailed a copy of the first grand jury transcript, with vouching on the first page, five days later. As Judge Perry noted , he would have had to approve re-presenting the case after a no-bill, and it’s “unfathomable” that he would have done so without “the best evidence available to him about what went wrong in the grand jury.” And in August, the government conceded there had been ‘discussions’ with Main Justice about ‘case updates,’ and earlier this month…

items.title: Court Tells Cops That The 4th Amendment Doesn’t Cover AI-Generated ‘Probable Cause’
items.summary:
I don’t know where this decision will take us, but its implications reach much further than the single case it covers. AI is pretty much everywhere, and if a court says an algorithm can’t make probable cause determinations, it affects/infects everything from facial recognition tech to predictive policing software to Axon adding AI shovelware to its omnipresent body cameras under the (correct) assumption cops don’t like writing reports.

In this case, Alain Osorio was arrested for allegedly passing a bad check at local bank. The only pictures of the suspect came from the bank’s CCTV footage. This was handed over to Detective Ryan Kilmer of the Florence (KY) Police Department.

The detective decided to run a screenshot of the suspect’s face (derived from the CCTV footage) through the PD’s facial recognition program. The decision [PDF] doesn’t specify which facial recognition program was used, but given that the match was made using photos found on Facebook, it suggests Clearview AI might have been involved, given its scraping of hundreds of billions of images from the open web since its inception.

Not that it did anything useful in terms of actual detective work. Nor did it do anything remotely constitutional, not when the operative word in “probable cause” is “probable.”

Relying solely on the AI identification, Detective Kilmer concluded that the match was accurate. [Id. at 4–5]. items.title: The Failure To Protect Our Soldiers
items.summary:
On this episode of The Jabot, I am joined by Saira Mohamed, the Agnes Roddy Robb Chair in Jurisprudence, Ethics, and Social Responsibility and a professor of law at the University of California, Berkeley. She’s the author of What a Country Owes Its Soldiers . After the get-to-know questions, we get into the nitty-gritty of her argument.

Mohamed argues that a government owes service members the same duties it owes everyone under its control, including protection from unnecessary dangers and from illegal orders. We talk about the Feres Doctrine, the myth of the volunteer, exploitation, legal remedies, and readiness.

Key Takeaways 
* Mohamed argues that a country owes its soldiers the same duties it owes every person under its authority and control.

* Military service is necessarily dangerous, but she says that doesn’t make every danger necessary, and the government owes a duty to avoid the unnecessary ones.

* The Feres Doctrine, read broadly, bars service members and their survivors from suing for injuries sustained in service, which Mohamed calls a very strange rule.

“They signed up for it” falls short, she says, because service members can’t simply quit and can be prosecuted for leaving.

Mohamed sees cultural change, understanding soldiers as people and not instruments, as the step that comes before any legal fix.

Kathryn Rubino is a Senior Editor at Above the Law, host of  The Jabot podcast , and co-host of  Thinking Like A Lawyer . AtL tipsters are the best, so please connect with her. Feel free to email  her  with any tips, questions, or comments and follow her…
items.t: The Failure To Protect Our Soldiers

items.title: Forget Impeachment, Just Stop Paying For Todd Blanche’s DOJ
items.summary:
Since the euphoria of the midterms has worn off, the left has been struggling to show what exactly can be done from both chambers of Congress to slow down the MAGA machine. Stopping MAGA judge picks is great and all, but that doesn’t keep the momentum of the blue tsunami alive.

Enter Eric Segall. 

Segall — a Georgia State University College of Law professor who worked in the Justice Department during George H.W. Bush’s administration, including on the Iran-Contra investigation — has a proposal in MS NOW this week that skips the hand-wringing: Congress should defund Trump’s DOJ. Not hold another round of oversight hearings. Not wait on criminal referrals to a department that has the exclusive power to bring federal charges and, as Segall notes, will never use it on its own people…. just turn off the money.

“Once Democrats control Congress, the most effective way to address the DOJ’s dysfunction is to threaten the White House using the power of the purse,” Segall writes.

The Appropriations Clause is about as plain as the Constitution gets: “No Money shall be drawn from the Treasury, but in Consequence of Appropriations made by Law.” A bill that actually slashes the DOJ’s budget would need the Senate and would face a veto. But the House doesn’t need anyone’s permission to not appropriate money. So Segall’s play is for the House to refuse to fund most of the department’s work until Attorney General Todd Blanche and FBI Director Kash Patel are gone. The goal, as he puts it, is to “force more moderate and less partisan leadership at the Justice Department.”

Would that risk…
items.t: Forget Impeachment, Just Stop Paying For Todd Blanche’s DOJ

items.title: Firms Want AI To Save Hours, Clients Want AI To Save Dollars — They Aren’t The Same Number
items.summary:
There’s always a little slippage between clients and outside counsel, but if you want to see a real chasm fracture the legal world, go watch a legal technology conference with programming evenly split between in-house and law firms. After everyone dutifully sings the praises of artificial intelligence and its transformative potential for the legal industry, the two tracks diverge dramatically.

Legal Innovators New York , put on by Artificial Lawyer and Cosmonauts , took over the Quorum by Convene space at 1221 Avenue of the Americas this week to talk about legal tech. Law firms on day one, in-house on day two.

Attendees, like me, who stayed for both days watched how the exact same technology prompts two very different responses.

On day one, Pillsbury’s Zorik Pesochinsky and Kristin Lorieo pulled out their crystal ball and predicted that clients will keep more work in-house and trim outside counsel lists over the next two to three years. If that’s true, they argued, firms needs to get out of their “defensive crouch” and start distilling what differentiates their work from client DIY hobbyists. The vision for outside counsel involves building out AI-enabled workflows that generate discrete deliverables — case assessment, deposition prep, witness prep — at fixed, predictable prices.

But, of course, not everything lends itself to fixed prices. Walking through the booth-lined hallway on that first day, the conversations tended toward words like “accelerate” and “deep.” To the extent AI wants to be the billable hour’s bodyguard , its interview is built on these terms. Work…

When Giuffra and Miller took over, S&C went in a new direction , establishing co-chairs for the first time. But that wasn’t really the headline for the Giuffra/Miller era at the firm.

With all due respect to Miller, the half of the partnership who did not spend the last two years as Donald Trump’s personal lawyer, the story here is Giuffra. He has been the face of S&C’s Trump era since the start. Back in Trump’s first term, S&C was reportedly one of the firms that told him no. items.title: Litigation Boutique Offering Bonuses Up To $247K

It’s that time of year when Biglaw starts en masse announcing its compensation news basking in all the commentary about their generosity. Then there’s always a boutique that shows up to absolutely dominate the prevailing Biglaw market scale and remind everyone that playing follow-the-leader with Cravath is merely a suggestion.

The latest is Pallas Partners, the transatlantic trial boutique founded by former Boies Schiller managing partner Natasha Harrison. Well… technically… Pallas is a pair of separate and distinct trial boutiques on either side of the Atlantic. Vagaries of business structure aside, the point is the firm just announced associate bonuses this year will top out at $247,000. That figure lands $92,000 more than the $155,000 Cravath put on the table for its most senior associates. 

Pallas builds its bonuses like a building, setting the market as the ground floor and working from there. Associates who hit the firm’s 2,000-hour target get the Cravath year-end bonus plus the Cravath special bonus, dollar for dollar:

Class Year 2026 Base Market Bonus Special Bonus 2025 $20,000 $11,000 2024 $30,000 $15,000 2023 $57,500 $20,000 2022 $75,000 $30,000 2021 $90,000 $40,000 2020 $105,000 $40,000 2019+ $115,000 $40,000 

But then, continuing the building analogy, come the stairs. Every additional block of hours unlocks a percentage hike on top of the base bonus, all the way up to an extra 80 percent at 2,500 hours:

items.title: Criminal law is constitutional law
items.summary:
With arguments over the Second Amendment and the Excessive Fines Clause on the near horizon, this column seeks to provide some tranquil and more generalized ideas – a moment of Thanksgiving holiday respite. Whether you are a Supreme Court follower who usually shunts criminal law to the side, or an experienced criminal law reader who might enjoy some holiday dinner thoughts for your friends and family, this column seeks to demonstrate that much of criminal law is actually constitutional law – and perhaps show why that can be so interesting. To do so, I will scatter some examples from last term, drawn from my recently published Annual Review of the Supreme Court’s Term, Criminal Cases booklet. When explaining criminal law to your friends or just opining over Thanksgiving dinner, I’d like to show why your mantra should be “crim law is con law” and vice versa .

Winship – criminal law fundamentals are constitutional law 

Every criminal law class I have taught over 40 years, from 1L first semester through advanced criminal procedure or federal criminal law, has begun with the same case: 1970’s In re Winship . Even non-lawyers know from film and TV that the prosecution’s high burden for proof in a criminal case is beyond a reasonable doubt. But do they know that this is constitutionally required? And perhaps more interesting, that this standard is nowhere, textually, in that document?

items.t: Criminal law is constitutional law

University of North Carolina , holding that race-conscious admissions at Harvard and the University of North Carolina violated the Constitution. Chief Justice John Roberts’ majority opinion in the case, along with Justice Brett Kavanaugh’s concurrence , cited Justice Sandra Day O’Connor’s 2003 prediction in Grutter v. Bollinger that “25 years from now, the use of racial preferences will no longer be necessary to further” student body diversity.

But the justices did not account for one thing, according to Brooklyn Law School Professor Yuvraj Joshi : O’Connor’s later misgivings about that statement. In interviews with her biographer after she left the court, O’Connor acknowledged that the 25-year figure “may have been a misjudgment.” When asked for a new estimate, she replied, “[t]here’s no timetable. You just don’t know.”
items.t: Even justices have regrets

items.title: The Settlement Mill Is The Part Of Personal Injury Law Nobody Wants To Talk About
items.summary:
There is a term lawyers sometimes use when talking among themselves that you probably won’t find on a law firm’s website.

Settlement mill.

It’s not a particularly flattering description, and that’s the point. It generally refers to a personal injury practice that operates on volume. Bring in as many cases as possible, move them through a relatively standardized process, negotiate settlements, collect fees, and make room for the next group of clients.

Now, I want to be careful here because I think this subject deserves considerably more thought than it usually gets.

Settling personal injury cases is not a bad thing. Quite the opposite. Most cases settle, and many absolutely should. Litigation can be expensive, emotionally exhausting, and painfully slow. A fair settlement can put money into the hands of an injured person when it is needed most, without the uncertainty of asking a jury to decide what happens next.

I’ve recommended settlements throughout my career. I’ve also advised clients against accepting offers that, in my judgment, failed to account for what they had lost.

Both decisions are part of doing the job properly.

My concern is what happens when settling cases becomes less about professional judgment and more about keeping a business operation moving.

And I think we need to talk about that.

When the Business Gets Bigger Than the Case

The battle over the Temporary Protected Status program – which allows foreign nationals to remain in the United States and work here when they cannot safely return home – returned to the Supreme Court on Wednesday afternoon. Specifically, the Trump administration asked the justices to block a September 2025 ruling by a federal judge in San Francisco that kept the program in place for Venezuelan nationals. U.S. Solicitor General D. John Sauer told the court that if they do not act, the order by U.S. District Judge Edward Chen “will spring into effect, inflicting severe and immediate harm.”

Then-DHS Secretary Alejandro Mayorkas designated Venezuela for the TPS program in 2021 and again in 2023. In 2025, he announced that the program would be extended through October 2026. Mayorkas cited a “severe humanitarian emergency” resulting from the “severe political and economic crisis” in Venezuela as the reason for the designation.

After Mayorkas’ successor, Kristi Noem, announced her decisions to end Venezuela’s designation and its subsequent extension, a group representing TPS holders went to federal court in San Francisco to challenge those decisions. Chen set them aside, and the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 9th Circuit upheld that ruling. In 2025, while that litigation was moving forward, the Supreme Court paused Chen’s order with regard to Venezuela, effectively clearing the way for the Trump administration to deport Venezuelan TPS beneficiaries while the case continued.

items.title: Calls for court packing fail the test of history
items.summary:
Please note that SCOTUS Outside Opinions constitute the views of outside contributors and do not reflect the opinions of SCOTUSblog or its staff. 

***

As Democrats have taken control in Congress, we can expect calls for court packing to intensify. One especially prominent proposal has been to expand the court to 13 justices. In the last few months, we have seen former Vice President Kamala Harris say the Supreme Court should be increased to this number. In August, Rep. James Clyburn, a longtime Democratic leader in the House, endorsed this proposal on “Meet the Press.” Just in the past few weeks, Hillary Clinton said the party “should seriously look at expanding the court while the Democrats are in power.” Potential presidential candidate Pete Buttigieg has advocated increasing the number of justices to 13 as well.

Some of these calls come with superficially plausible justifications. Take Hillary Clinton’s proposal, for instance. “It used to be that you’d have one justice for each circuit,” Clinton explained. “We now have 13 circuits, we should have 13 justices.” Buttigieg has also argued for modifying the size of the court on that basis. But the symmetry argument is pretextual: It is no mere coincidence that the reintroduction of a one-to-one justice to circuit relationship under Democratic control would produce exactly the four seats needed to transform the current six-to-three conservative majority into a seven-to-six liberal one. Such a proposal then allows advocates to cover their desire for change to the court’s size in the language of a seemingly neutral…
items.t: Calls for court packing fail the test of history

items.title: Five major issues that may still make it onto this term’s oral argument docket
items.summary:
Time is running out for the justices to add cases to this term’s oral argument docket . Under the Supreme Court’s typical briefing schedule , a case must be granted by mid-January to be briefed in time for the final argument session, which begins this term on April 19.

But despite being short on time, the justices are not short on major petitions for review . Over the next two months, they will likely consider petitions addressing such high-profile issues as the Trump administration’s ban on transgender servicemembers, state laws requiring Ten Commandments displays in public school classrooms, and the regulation of prediction markets like Kalshi.

Understanding the timeline 

Before we explore some of the major issues pending before the Supreme Court, let me first offer a brief refresher on how a petition for review makes it to the oral argument docket. (For more on this process, read law professor Stephen Wermiel’s SCOTUSblog column from last week.)

Litigants file a petition for review, also known as a petition for certiorari, at the Supreme Court when they want the justices to review a lower court ruling against them. In their petition, they lay out, among other things, their views on why the ruling was wrong and why the issue is worthy of the justices’ attention.

After a petition is filed, the litigants that prevailed before the lower court (known as the respondents) have 30 days to respond, although they may ask for additional time. Sometimes, they file a brief in which they agree that the Supreme Court should take up the issue, but it’s far more common for…

items.title: The Supreme Court before it stood apart
items.summary:
The Political Supreme Court: A Forgotten History by Rachel A. Shelden (The University of North Carolina Press)

***

In her excellent new book,  The Political Supreme Court: A Forgotten History , professor Rachel Shelden closes with Chief Justice John Roberts’ insistence that “you don’t want the political branches telling you what the law is,” and that public opinion should not guide the court’s decisions.

That will likely sound quite familiar: it is how we have come to think about the Supreme Court. But Shelden’s history shows that the 19th century court and the way Americans perceived it were very different. Indeed, the modern idea of the detached judge, the justice as apolitical “ umpire ,” is not nearly as  originalist  as we tend to assume.

Shelden opens with Abraham Lincoln arguing before the court in 1849. The court that Lincoln and his fellow members of the bar knew was not the marble institution, removed from ordinary political life, that we picture today. For example, the justices “rode circuit.” Each was assigned a region, generally the part of the country from which he hailed and in which he traveled through to preside over federal trial courts. This brought the justices into regular contact with local lawyers, officials, and communities.

Shelden calls this “judicial representation”: the idea that a justice would bring a region’s perspective to the court because he knew the people he impliedly represented. Although today’s justices are assigned to a circuit, typically the circuit to which they have ties geographically, the concept is now decidedly different;…

items.title: An election impact on the Supreme Court’s immigration docket
items.summary:
The effect of this month’s elections is likely to impact immigration policy over the coming years as politicians and political analysts assess how reactions to the Trump administration’s immigration law enforcement tactics affected voters’ preferences. But the significant shift towards Democrats in states previously controlled by Republicans is likely to impact immigration law even sooner. The Supreme Court is currently considering whether to add to its calendar a case about the constitutionality of an immigration law enacted by Iowa in 2024 . The justices had previously signaled their openness to weighing in, but the state’s Republican attorney general, who asked the court to hear the case, lost her reelection bid to a Democrat, casting doubt on the case’s future.

Iowa’s Senate File 2340 criminalizes certain immigration conduct. For example, anyone who has previously been excluded or deported from the United States by federal immigration officials but “ is at any time found ” in Iowa can be convicted of an aggravated misdemeanor and imprisoned for up to two years . As an alternative to potential conviction, the law allows a state judge overseeing a criminal prosecution to order the defendant to leave the United States. Anyone who fails to leave as required can be convicted of a felony and imprisoned for as much as 10 years .

items.title: All eyes on the justices’ next private conference
items.summary:
The Senate confirmed Justice Joseph Story to the Supreme Court on this day in 1811. When he joined three months later at age 32, he became the youngest justice in Supreme Court history, as we noted in a Closer Look in May.

At the Court On Tuesday, the Supreme Court indicated that several notable petitions for review will be considered at the justices’ next private conference on Friday, Dec. 4. The disputes address such issues as the Trump administration’s ban on transgender servicemembers and its approach to appointing acting U.S. attorneys. For more on the conference, see the On Site section below.

The December argument session will begin on Monday, Nov. 30.

items.title: Justices to consider disputes over transgender servicemembers, E. Jean Carroll’s jury award, and acting U.S. attorneys at next private conference
items.summary:
The justices of the Supreme Court aren’t scheduled to meet for a private conference – and vote on new petitions for review – for two-and-a-half weeks. But when they do, on Friday, Dec. 4, they will have a number of high-profile cases to consider – which could, in turn, lead to a busy spring.

The federal government and President Donald Trump are at the center of three of the biggest petitions for review up for consideration on Dec. 4.

In United States v. Talbott , the justices will decide whether to review a ruling by a federal appeals court in Washington, D.C., that bars the Trump administration from expelling several transgender servicemembers from the military.

In the government’s petition for review , U.S. Solicitor General D. John Sauer called the decision by the U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit “gravely erroneous” and argued that its “reasoning cannot be squared with this Court’s precedents or deference to the military.”

The challengers urged the court to stay out of the dispute, calling the D.C. Circuit’s decision “narrow” and temporary. And in any event, they added, the ruling is correct, because the Trump administration’s ban on transgender servicemembers was motivated by hostility to transgender people rather than “military judgments.”

In another case to be considered, Trump and the federal government have each filed petitions for review in connection with Trump’s challenge to the $83.3 million verdict entered against him in a lawsuit brought by E.
